title: The gatekeeper
hook: mindfulness is like the wise gatekeeper of a frontier fortress (AN 7, the fortress)

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma sati, right mindfulness, and your line, remember to notice. Did a doorway remind you once: body, feeling, mind? Day three hundred ninety.

At the edge of a kingdom, where the road comes in from foreign land, stands a fortress. Thick walls. A moat. Soldiers. Storerooms of grain and oil. And at the gate, one person whose whole job is to look at every face that arrives and decide: you, come in; you, I don't know you, wait outside. Everything inside depends on that one person paying attention. The Buddha drew this fortress in detail, piece by piece. Today: the gatekeeper.
screen: `A FORTRESS ON THE FRONTIER.` → `WALLS, MOAT, SOLDIERS, STORES.` → `ONE PERSON AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the book of sevens of the Numbered Discourses. A king's frontier fortress, the Buddha says, can't be taken by enemies from outside when it has seven things in place and four kinds of provisions stored. Then he maps each piece onto a practitioner. The deep-rooted pillar at the entrance is faith. The moat is a sense of shame about doing wrong. The path patrolled around the walls is fear of wrongdoing. The weapons are learning, the teachings you've heard. The army is energy. The high, thick rampart is wisdom. And the gatekeeper, wise, experienced and intelligent, who keeps strangers out and lets known friends in, is mindfulness. Notice what the gatekeeper does and doesn't do. He doesn't fight; that's the army's job. He doesn't build the walls. He knows who's who, and he's at his post. Mindfulness, in this picture, is what recognizes what's arriving. That's anger, coming up the road. That's kindness, a friend: open the gate. Without the gatekeeper, the strongest walls are useless. The enemy simply walks in, because no one noticed. A few days ago you guarded the sense doors. This is the same gate, seen from inside the walls, and it echoes a Dhammapada line from the first year, in Max Müller's words: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." A frontier fort, not a palace. Mindfulness stands where ordinary life arrives.
screen: `SEVEN DEFENSES, FOUR STORES.` · `PILLAR, MOAT, WEAPONS, ARMY, WALL.` · `THE GATEKEEPER KNOWS WHO'S WHO.` · `WHERE ORDINARY LIFE ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE GATEKEEPER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and picture yourself at the gate. Thoughts and moods come up the road, one at a time. As each one arrives, just name it, the way a gatekeeper would: worry. Planning. A memory. Irritation. Tenderness. Don't fight any of them. Just recognize them. If you like, let the friendly ones in, and let the strangers wait outside. Your only job is to stay at your post. The bell holds the time.
The gatekeeper. In the book of sevens, mindfulness is the wise gatekeeper of the frontier fortress, the one who knows who's who.
Your line: the gatekeeper. Today, be your own gatekeeper: when a mood arrives, name it before you let it in. Day three hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Meditation teachers often use the gatekeeper image to describe mindfulness as noticing and naming what arises, and some traditions practice mental noting, labeling each thought or feeling as it appears.

fork.setup: you're the gatekeeper. irritation arrives, dressed up as "just being honest." what's your job?
options: recognize him, and keep him outside.
fork.reveal: in the fortress simile the gatekeeper doesn't fight; he knows strangers from friends, keeping out the one and admitting the other.

original.note: Pali dovārika: gatekeeper, the image for mindfulness in the fortress simile.

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness means emptying the mind.
what it means: recognizing what's arriving, so you can choose what to let in.

what a scholar hears: in the fortress sutta (AN 7.67, or 7.63 in some editions) the seven requisites are faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, learning, energy, mindfulness and wisdom, and the four stores of food stand for the four jhānas.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 7.67 (Nagaropama Sutta, the fortress; 7.63 in some editions)

notes: Check Müller's exact wording of Dhammapada 315 in SBE 10.

AN 7.67 paraphrased: pillar = faith, moat = hiri (shame), patrol path = ottappa (fear of wrongdoing), weapons = learning, army = energy, gatekeeper = mindfulness, rampart = wisdom; four foods = four jhānas. Confirm the mapping and numbering.
Year one day 215 ('The frontier fort') used Dhammapada 315; the script points back to it.
